teaser: A turning tip. A spiral path. Where do the chips go?
title: How Drill Bits Work
question: Why does a spiral move things when it spins?
idea: A drill bit’s cutting lips shave off chips. Its spiral flutes carry the chips up and out as it turns.

curiosity.intro: A twist in a metal rod gives tiny chips a way out.
curiosity.carryForward: Follow a spiral from the workbench to the garden and back.

questions.question: Which part makes the hole?
questions.notice: Look at the cutting edges at the tip.
questions.say: A twist drill bit is a metal rod with spiral grooves. As it turns and moves into the material, the cutting lips at its tip shave off tiny bits called chips.
questions.try: Trace the tip in the picture, then follow one spiral groove.

questions.question: Where do the chips go?
questions.notice: Follow the chips from the bottom of the hole to the top.
questions.say: The spiral grooves are called flutes. They help carry chips up and out as the bit turns, keeping the hole clear. The cutting lips make chips; the flutes give them a way out.
questions.try: Use the diorama to follow one chip up the flute.

questions.question: What can we notice by turning slowly?
questions.notice: Look for a curl beside the screw thread.
questions.say: A screw has a spiral ridge called a thread. It acts like a ramp wrapped around the rod. Turning against the material helps the screw move in. A screw thread is a raised ridge; a drill flute is a groove.
questions.try: With Big close by, hand-turn a screw slowly into soap or clay on a tray and look at the curls. Power drills are tools for adults; kids do not use them. Big stays close. Try turning a pencil in an enclosed hand sharpener, too.

questions.question: What else can a turning spiral move?
questions.notice: Water rides from a low bowl to a higher cup.
questions.say: An auger lifts loose soil or ice from a hole. An Archimedes screw lifts pockets of water along a sloping tube. A spiral slopes along its length, so turning against material can push or carry that material along. It needs something to work against, not just empty space.
questions.try: Wrap a ribbon around a pencil and follow its sloping path with your eyes.

beats.title: A spiral to follow
beats.passage: Little Wonderer leaned toward the magnifier. A drill bit rested on the bench. This metal rod had a spiral shape that wound around and along it. “Why all the twists?” Little asked. Big pointed to the tip. Its cutting lips are edges that shave off tiny bits of material as the bit turns.
beats.prompt: How does the tip’s job differ from the spiral’s job?

foldable.heading: Follow the spiral
foldable.body: Little found a spiral on a drill bit. As the bit turns, the cutting lips at its tip shave off tiny chips.

beats.title: A thread in the soap
beats.passage: Big slowly turned a screw into a bar of soap by hand. Little watched a pale curl gather beside it. A screw thread is a spiral ridge around a screw. As it turns against the material, the sloping thread helps pull the screw farther in. Turning can make something move along, too.
beats.prompt: How could a sloping thread help a screw move in?

foldable.heading: A thread in soap
foldable.body: Big turned a screw into soap. Its thread wound around like a tiny ramp, helping the screw move in with each turn.

beats.title: A way out for chips
beats.passage: Their cutaway display showed inside a hole. The drill bit’s sharp tip and cutting lips made small shavings called chips. Its spiral grooves, called flutes, gave those chips a path up and out as the bit turned. “Like a spiral slide going up!” said Little. The hole needed room for the next chips.
beats.prompt: Why does the hole need a path for chips to leave?

foldable.heading: A way out
foldable.body: Chips need a way out of the hole. The drill bit’s spiral grooves, called flutes, carry them up as it turns.

beats.title: A spiral in the soil
beats.passage: At the garden bench, Big showed Little an auger. An auger is a tool with a broad spiral for making holes in soil or ice. Its lower edge loosens material. Turning lifts the loose bits along the spiral. Little traced the path in the notebook: around, up, and out of the hole.
beats.prompt: What do a drill bit and an auger both move out?

foldable.heading: Around and up
foldable.body: An auger has a broad spiral. As it turns in the soil, it lifts loose dirt up and out of the hole.

beats.title: Water takes a ride
beats.passage: Back at the table, a sloping tube joined a low bowl to a high cup. Inside was an Archimedes screw, a large spiral that can lift water. Big turned its handle. Pockets of water rode up between the spiral and the tube. Little watched water reach the cup above the bowl.
beats.prompt: How does turning help water reach a higher cup?

foldable.heading: Water takes a ride
foldable.body: Big turned the Archimedes screw. Pockets of water rode up the sloping tube and spilled into a cup higher than the bowl.

beats.title: What else can turn?
beats.passage: Little found more turning tools. A corkscrew spirals into a cork to pull it out. Egg-beater gears make a hand-crank spin the beaters faster. A hand sharpener shaves pencil curls. Little drew a spiral. “Why does a spiral move things when it spins?”
beats.prompt: Which tools move material along, and which mainly spin it?

foldable.heading: Keep a question
foldable.body: Little drew a spiral beside the turning tools. “Why does a spiral move things when it spins?” The notebook had room to wonder.

math.title: Turning-tool stories
math.intro: Read each little story. Decide whether to add or subtract.
math.actionLabel: Solve one step at a time

tasks.prompt: Little counts 24 screws in a jar. Big adds 17 more. How many screws are in the jar now?
tasks.hint: Add the two groups. You can make a new ten.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: Big has 63 screws and puts 28 into a box. How many screws stay in the jar?
tasks.hint: Start with the whole group and take away the screws put in the box.
tasks.worked: 63 − 28 = 35 screws. Take away 20 to get 43, then take away 8.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: Little counts 16 turns of a hand crank, then 27 more turns. How many turns does Little count altogether?
tasks.hint: Add the turns from both rounds.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: There are 54 pencil curls on a tray. Little brushes 22 into a paper bag. How many curls remain on the tray?
tasks.hint: Subtract the curls that leave the tray.
tasks.worked: 54 − 22 = 32 curls. Take away 20 to get 34, then take away 2.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: Big turns an egg-beater handle 38 times, then 15 more times. How many handle turns does Big make in all?
tasks.hint: Add the first turns and the extra turns.
tasks.worked: 38 + 15 = 53 turns. Add 10 to get 48, then add 5.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: A sand tray holds 71 small scoops of sand. A hand auger lifts out 34 scoops. How many scoops of sand remain?
tasks.hint: Take away the scoops lifted out of the tray.
tasks.worked: 71 − 34 = 37 scoops. Take away 30 to get 41, then take away 4.
tasks.label: TASK 6

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: Cutting lips shave off chips, and flutes carry the chips out. Removing chips leaves space for more material to be shaved.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: A screw thread is a raised spiral ridge that helps the screw move in. A flute is a spiral groove that gives chips a way out.

answers.label: Reading · 3
answers.text: Both use a turning spiral to carry material along: an auger lifts loose soil or ice, and an Archimedes screw lifts water.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept a clear command spoken, dictated, drawn, or written. Example: “Turn the screw slowly into the soap, then look at the curls on the thread.”

parentGuidance: Age 8, Grade 3 reading, Grade 2 math. Power drills are grown-up tools; kids do not use them. A grown-up stays close and leads the soap or clay activity, placing the material on a tray and choosing the screw. Use an enclosed hand pencil sharpener for the pencil-curl observation. The illustrated drill bit is a common twist bit. Its cutting lips remove material; flutes provide chip clearance as the bit rotates and advances. The diorama isolates chip travel in a fixed cutaway, with enlarged chips and a shortened path. Real chip shapes and motion depend on the material and bit. Screw threads are raised ridges, unlike the recessed flutes. A turning spiral needs contact or confinement to move material along. The egg beater uses gears for faster rotation; it does not lift material like an auger.
